title: Two Sum
prompt: Write a function `solve(nums, target)` that returns the indices of the two numbers that add up to target, using a hashmap for O(n) time.
concept: Single-pass hashmap: check if target-n is already in the map BEFORE inserting n. Inserting first then checking causes a false self-match when a value appears once but happens to equal target/2.

title: Sliding window max sum
prompt: Write `solve(nums, k)` returning the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of length k.
concept: Maintain a running window sum: add the incoming element, subtract the outgoing one, O(n) total. Recomputing sum(window) on every step is the O(n*k) trap that still passes small inputs.

title: Restaurant 7-day moving average
prompt: Table `Customer(customer_id, name, visited_on, amount)` (multiple customers can visit on the same day). Collapse to one total per visited_on date, then — starting from the 7th distinct date onward — return visited_on, amount (the sum of that day's total plus the 6 preceding days' totals), and average_amount (that sum divided by 7, rounded to 2 decimals). Order by visited_on.
concept: A window SUM with `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` over the per-day totals gives a trailing 7-day sum directly; ROW_NUMBER() over the same date ordering identifies which days actually have 6 full prior days available, since the first 6 distinct dates can't form a complete 7-day window.

title: Products ordered in a period

title: Most active rater and top February movie

concept: Each half is computed independently — one grouped by user_id counting ratings, the other grouped by movie_id averaging rating filtered to February 2020 — then UNION ALL stacks the two single-row results into one results column instead of trying to force both computations into a single GROUP BY.

A customer qualifies as a 'golden hour' customer when all of: they have at least 3 orders total; at least 60% of their orders fall in peak hours, defined as the order's time-of-day being 11:00-13:59 or 18:00-20:59; at least 50% of their orders carry a rating; and the average rating among only their rated orders is at least 4.0. Return customer_id, total_orders, peak_hour_percentage (rounded to 2 decimals), average_rating (rounded to 2 decimals), ordered by average_rating descending, then customer_id descending.
concept: strftime('%H', order_timestamp) pulls just the hour out of a full datetime string so peak-hour membership becomes a plain BETWEEN check; every qualification rule is a per-customer ratio computed from conditional SUMs over the same group, so all four conditions can live in one WHERE clause applied after a single GROUP BY.

title: Loyal customers by purchase pattern
prompt: Table `customer_transactions(transaction_id, customer_id, transaction_date, amount, transaction_type)` where transaction_type is 'purchase' or 'refund'. A customer is 'loyal' when all of: they have at least 3 'purchase' transactions; the span between their earliest and latest transaction_date is at least 30 days; and their refund rate — refund count divided by (purchase count + refund count) — is below 20%. Return the customer_id of every loyal customer, ordered ascending.
concept: julianday(MAX(date)) - julianday(MIN(date)) turns a date span into a plain day-count difference; the refund rate is built from two conditional SUMs over the same grouped rows rather than a second query, so the whole qualification check fits in one HAVING clause.

title: Subscribers at risk of churn
prompt: Table `subscription_events(event_id, user_id, event_date, event_type, plan_name, monthly_amount)` where event_type is 'start', 'upgrade', 'downgrade', or 'cancel' (plan_name is NULL and monthly_amount is 0 on a cancel event). A user is at 'churn risk' when all of: their most recent event (by event_date) is not a cancel; they have had at least one downgrade event; their current monthly_amount, taken from that most recent event, is less than 50% of the highest monthly_amount they have ever had; and the gap between their first and last event_date is at least 60 days. Return user_id, current_plan, current_monthly_amount, max_historical_amount, days_as_subscriber, ordered by days_as_subscriber descending, then user_id ascending.
concept: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_date DESC) isolates each user's single most recent row so its plan/amount/type can be compared against separately-computed full-history aggregates (MAX(monthly_amount), the date span) — mixing 'latest row only' logic with 'all rows' aggregates in one query needs this kind of window-plus-join split rather than one flat GROUP BY.

title: Students improving between exams
prompt: Table `Scores(student_id, subject, score, exam_date)`. A student-subject pairing counts as 'improved' when the student took at least 2 exams in that subject and their score on the latest exam_date is strictly higher than their score on the earliest exam_date. Return student_id, subject, first_score, last_score, and improvement (last_score - first_score), ordered by student_id ascending, then subject ascending.
concept: MIN(exam_date)/MAX(exam_date) locate the earliest and latest dates per (student, subject) group, but pulling the *score* recorded on those specific dates needs a self-join back to Scores on exam_date, since there's no built-in aggregate for 'the value paired with the smallest date'.

title: Employees with 3-review improving streaks
prompt: Tables `employees(employee_id, name)` and `performance_reviews(review_id, employee_id, review_date, rating)` (rating 1-5). An employee qualifies when they have at least 3 reviews and, looking only at their 3 most recent reviews by review_date, the ratings are strictly increasing from oldest to newest of those three. Return employee_id, name, and improvement_score (the newest of the 3 ratings minus the oldest of the 3), ordered by improvement_score descending, then name ascending.
concept: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY review_date DESC) labels each employee's reviews 1st, 2nd, 3rd... most recent; three self-joins pull the rn=1/2/3 rows back onto one line so their ratings can be compared directly, since 'the last 3 rows, in order' isn't something a single aggregate can express.

title: Patients who recovered from COVID
prompt: Tables `patients(patient_id, patient_name, age)` and `covid_tests(test_id, patient_id, test_date, result)` where result is 'Positive', 'Negative', or 'Inconclusive'. A patient has recovered if they have a Positive test followed by a later Negative test. Using each patient's first Positive test date and the first Negative test date after it, return patient_id, patient_name, age, and recovery_time (the day gap between those two dates), ordered by recovery_time ascending, then patient_name ascending.
concept: Two CTEs split the two-step lookup: one finds MIN(test_date) among Positive rows per patient, the second finds MIN(test_date) among Negative rows per patient filtered to test_date strictly after the first CTE's date — chaining a filtered MIN after another MIN is how 'first X after Y' is expressed without procedural row-by-row logic.

title: Drivers with improved fuel efficiency
prompt: Tables `drivers(driver_id, driver_name)` and `trips(trip_id, driver_id, trip_date, distance_km, fuel_consumed)`. For each driver with trips in both halves of the year (first half: Jan-Jun, second half: Jul-Dec), compute their average per-trip fuel efficiency (distance_km / fuel_consumed) in each half. Return driver_id, driver_name, first_half_avg, second_half_avg, and efficiency_improvement (second_half_avg - first_half_avg), all rounded to 2 decimals, ordered by efficiency_improvement descending, then driver_name ascending.
concept: A CASE expression on the trip month buckets every row into 'H1' or 'H2' before any aggregation happens; two AVG(CASE WHEN half=... THEN eff END) calls in the same GROUP BY then compute both half-averages side by side, and requiring both to be non-NULL is what enforces 'has trips in both halves.'

title: Employees overbooked with meetings
prompt: Tables `employees(employee_id, employee_name, department)` and `meetings(meeting_id, employee_id, meeting_date, meeting_type, duration_hours)`. Treat a standard work week as 40 hours; a week is 'meeting-heavy' for an employee if their total meeting duration that week exceeds 20 hours. Return employee_id, employee_name, department, and meeting_heavy_weeks (the count of such weeks), but only for employees with at least 2 meeting-heavy weeks, ordered by meeting_heavy_weeks descending, then employee_name ascending.
concept: strftime('%Y-%W', meeting_date) collapses each date to a year-week bucket, so summing duration_hours grouped by (employee_id, week) turns 'hours per week' into a normal aggregate; a second GROUP BY then counts how many of those weekly totals cleared the 20-hour bar.

title: Stores with an inventory imbalance
prompt: Tables `stores(store_id, store_name, location)` and `inventory(inventory_id, store_id, product_name, quantity, price)`. For stores stocking at least 3 different products, compare the store's single most expensive product to its single cheapest product. A store has an inventory imbalance if the most expensive product's quantity is lower than the cheapest product's quantity. Return store_id, store_name, location, most_exp_product, cheapest_product, and imbalance_ratio (cheapest quantity divided by most-expensive quantity, rounded to 2 decimals), ordered by imbalance_ratio descending, then store_name ascending.
concept: Two separate ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY price DESC) and ORDER BY price ASC windows pick out the single most-expensive and single-cheapest row per store in one pass, avoiding a MAX(price)/MIN(price) subquery pair that would need re-joining back to fetch the product_name and quantity for each extreme.

title: Books with polarized reader opinions
prompt: Tables `books(book_id, title, author, genre, pages)` and `reading_sessions(session_id, book_id, reader_name, pages_read, session_rating)` (rating 1-5). Consider only books with at least 5 reading sessions. A book has polarized opinions if it has at least one session rated 4 or higher and at least one rated 2 or lower, and at least 60% of its sessions fall into those two extreme bands. Return book_id, title, author, genre, pages, rating_spread (max rating minus min rating), and polarization_score (fraction of extreme-rated sessions, rounded to 2 decimals), ordered by polarization_score descending, then title descending.
concept: The 60% threshold and the 'has both extremes' rule are both derived from the same two conditional SUMs (ratings <=2, ratings >=4) over one GROUP BY — computing the fraction from those sums instead of a separate COUNT(*) subquery keeps every polarization rule anchored to the same per-book row count.

title: Users with high AI token usage
prompt: Table `prompts(user_id, prompt, tokens)`. For users who submitted at least 3 prompts, and who had at least one prompt using more tokens than their own average, return user_id, prompt_count (total prompts), and avg_tokens (average tokens, rounded to 2 decimals), ordered by avg_tokens descending, then user_id ascending.
concept: 'At least one value above the group's own average' never needs a per-row comparison subquery: whenever a group's values aren't all identical, its maximum is always strictly greater than its mean, so MAX(tokens) > AVG(tokens) in the HAVING clause is an exact, much cheaper substitute.

title: Emotionally consistent reaction users
prompt: Table `reactions(user_id, content_id, reaction)`. Consider only users who reacted to at least 5 different content items. A user is 'emotionally consistent' if their single most common reaction type accounts for at least 60% of all their reactions. Return user_id, dominant_reaction (their most frequent reaction type), and reaction_ratio (that reaction's share of their total, rounded to 2 decimals), ordered by reaction_ratio descending, then user_id ascending.
concept: Two grouped counts feed a window function: per-(user, reaction) counts and per-user totals are joined together, then ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY cnt DESC, reaction ASC) picks the single most frequent reaction per user (breaking ties alphabetically) so its ratio can be filtered against the 60% threshold.

title: Valid Parentheses
prompt: Write `solve(s)` returning whether the brackets in `s` (any mix of `()[]{}`) are balanced and correctly nested.
concept: Push opens onto a stack; on a close, pop and check it matches. A close with an empty stack, or a leftover stack at the end, means unbalanced — both are easy to forget.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
prompt: Write `solve(prices)` returning the max profit from one buy then one sell (buy must happen before sell); return 0 if no profit is possible.
concept: Track the minimum price seen so far in a single pass and compare against price-so_far minus that minimum. Computing every pair is O(n^2) and unnecessary.

title: Valid Palindrome
prompt: Write `solve(s)` returning whether `s` reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring case and non-alphanumeric characters.
concept: Filter to lowercase alphanumerics first, then compare the string to its reverse. Trying to two-pointer past punctuation inline is doable but easy to get off-by-one on.

title: Contains Duplicate
prompt: Write `solve(nums)` returning whether any value appears more than once in `nums`.
concept: A set dedupes in O(n); if its length is shorter than the list, something repeated. Sorting first also works but costs O(n log n) for no benefit.

title: Valid Anagram
prompt: Write `solve(s, t)` returning whether `t` is an anagram of `s` (same letters, same counts).
concept: Count letters of `s` into a hashmap, then decrement while scanning `t`; any negative or leftover count means it's not an anagram. Different lengths can be rejected immediately.

title: Missing Number
prompt: Write `solve(nums)` returning the one number missing from `nums`, a list containing n distinct numbers from `0` to `n`.
concept: The sum of `0..n` minus the actual sum of `nums` gives the missing value in O(n) with no extra space. XOR-ing all indices and values works too but the sum trick is simpler to reason about.

title: Climbing Stairs
prompt: Write `solve(n)` returning how many distinct ways to climb `n` stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
concept: This is Fibonacci in disguise: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), since the last step was either a 1-step or a 2-step. Track just the last two values instead of recursing to avoid exponential blowup.

title: Counting Bits
prompt: Write `solve(n)` returning a list where index `i` (for `0..n`) holds the number of 1-bits in `i`.
concept: `i`'s bit count equals the bit count of `i >> 1` plus `i`'s own last bit — a one-line DP recurrence off already-computed smaller values, avoiding recounting bits from scratch for every number.

title: Product of Array Except Self
prompt: Write `solve(nums)` returning a list where each element is the product of all other elements, without using division.
concept: Two passes: build running prefix products left-to-right, then multiply in running suffix products right-to-left. Using division breaks on zeros in the input, which is why it's disallowed.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
prompt: Write `solve(s)` returning the length of the longest substring of `s` with no repeated characters.
concept: Sliding window with a hashmap of last-seen index per character: when a repeat is found inside the current window, jump the window start past its previous occurrence instead of restarting from scratch.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
prompt: Write `solve(nums)` returning the length of the longest run of consecutive integers present in `nums`, in O(n) time.
concept: Put everything in a set, then only start counting a run from numbers whose predecessor (n-1) isn't in the set — that guarantees each run is walked exactly once instead of re-walked from every member.

title: Group Anagrams
prompt: Write `solve(strs)` grouping strings that are anagrams of each other, returning a list of groups.
concept: Anagrams share the same sorted-character key, so use that sorted string as a hashmap key and bucket originals under it — O(n * k log k) instead of comparing every pair.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
prompt: Write `solve(nums, k)` returning the `k` most frequent elements in `nums`.
concept: Bucket sort by frequency (bucket index = count, capped at len(nums)) beats a heap or full sort — frequencies are bounded by array length, so counting then reading buckets top-down is O(n).

title: Jump Game
prompt: Write `solve(nums)` returning whether you can reach the last index, starting at index 0, where `nums[i]` is the max jump length from `i`.
concept: Greedily track the farthest reachable index while scanning left to right; if the current index ever exceeds that farthest reach, it's unreachable. No need to try every jump combination.

title: Merge Intervals
prompt: Write `solve(intervals)` merging all overlapping intervals and returning the merged list.
concept: Sort by start first — then overlaps only ever happen between an interval and the one just placed before it, so a single left-to-right pass with a running "last merged" interval suffices.

title: Insert Interval
prompt: Write `solve(intervals, newInterval)` inserting `newInterval` into an already sorted, non-overlapping `intervals` list, merging as needed.
concept: Three phases in one pass: copy intervals that end before the new one starts, merge every interval that overlaps the new one into it, then copy the rest untouched.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
prompt: Write `solve(intervals)` returning the minimum number of intervals to remove so none of the rest overlap.
concept: Sort by end time and greedily keep an interval whenever it starts at or after the last kept interval's end — this is the classic activity-selection greedy, and sorting by start instead of end gives wrong answers.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
prompt: Write `solve(nums, target)` returning the index of `target` in a rotated ascending array (distinct values), or -1 if absent, in O(log n).
concept: Binary search still works: at each mid, one half is always normally sorted — check whether target falls in that half's range to decide which way to go, instead of trying to un-rotate the array first.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
prompt: Write `solve(nums)` returning the minimum value in a rotated ascending array (distinct values), in O(log n).
concept: Binary search on whether mid is left of the rotation point: if `nums[mid] > nums[hi]`, the minimum is to the right of mid; otherwise it's at mid or to the left. A linear scan works but throws away the sorted structure.

title: Container With Most Water
prompt: Write `solve(height)` returning the max area formed between two lines from `height`, where area = width * shorter height.
concept: Two pointers from both ends, always moving the shorter side inward: moving the taller side inward can only shrink width without ever increasing the limiting (shorter) height, so it never helps.

title: 3Sum
prompt: Write `solve(nums)` returning all unique triplets in `nums` that sum to zero.
concept: Sort first, fix one number, then two-pointer the rest for the remaining pair — sorting turns an O(n^3) triple loop into O(n^2), and skipping past equal adjacent values after a match is what keeps duplicates out.

title: Combination Sum
prompt: Write `solve(candidates, target)` returning all unique combinations (numbers may repeat) from `candidates` that sum to `target`.
concept: Backtrack with a start index that never moves backward, so the same number can be reused going forward but combinations aren't generated in more than one order. Sorting first lets you break early once a candidate exceeds the remaining target.

title: Coin Change
prompt: Write `solve(coins, amount)` returning the fewest coins needed to make `amount`, or -1 if impossible.
concept: Bottom-up DP: `dp[a]` is the min coins for amount `a`, built from `dp[a - coin] + 1` over every coin. Greedy (always take the biggest coin) fails on coin sets like [1,3,4] for amount 6.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
prompt: Write `solve(nums)` returning the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of `nums`.
concept: Maintain a `tails` list where `tails[i]` is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length i+1; binary-search each new number's spot in it. This gets O(n log n) versus the O(n^2) DP of comparing every prior pair.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
prompt: Write `solve(text1, text2)` returning the length of the longest subsequence common to both strings.
concept: Classic 2D DP: `dp[i][j]` is the LCS length of the first `i` and `j` characters. Matching characters extend the diagonal; otherwise take the best of dropping one character from either string.

title: House Robber
prompt: Write `solve(nums)` returning the max sum obtainable from `nums` without picking two adjacent elements.
concept: Track only the best-so-far excluding vs including the previous house, rolling forward — full O(n) space DP is unnecessary since each step only needs the last two values.

title: House Robber II
prompt: Write `solve(nums)` returning the max sum obtainable from a circular arrangement of houses, without picking two adjacent (first and last count as adjacent).
concept: Since the first and last house can't both be taken, the answer is the better of two linear house-robber runs: one excluding the first house, one excluding the last. Handle the single-house case separately since both slices would be empty otherwise.

title: Word Break
prompt: Write `solve(s, wordDict)` returning whether `s` can be segmented into a sequence of words from `wordDict`.
concept: DP where `dp[i]` means the prefix `s[:i]` is fully segmentable: it's true if some earlier `dp[j]` is true and `s[j:i]` is a dictionary word. A greedy first-match approach fails when an early match blocks a later valid split.

title: Decode Ways
prompt: Write `solve(s)` returning how many ways a digit string `s` (mapping 'A'-'Z' to 1-26) can be decoded.
concept: DP where `dp[i]` sums the ways using the last digit alone (if nonzero) and the last two digits as a pair (if 10-26). A leading zero anywhere with no valid pairing to absorb it kills that whole branch.

title: Unique Paths
prompt: Write `solve(m, n)` returning how many distinct paths a robot has from the top-left to bottom-right of an m x n grid, moving only right or down.
concept: 1D rolling DP: `dp[j]` accumulates paths to column `j` as the row scan progresses, since a cell's path count is just the sum of the cell above and the cell to the left. Full recursion recomputes the same subgrids exponentially.

title: Number of 1 Bits
prompt: Write `solve(n)` returning the count of 1-bits in the binary representation of integer `n`.
concept: Shift and mask one bit at a time, adding `n & 1` and shifting right — the `n & (n-1)` trick (clears the lowest set bit) is a faster variant worth knowing but not required for correctness here.

title: Reverse Bits
prompt: Write `solve(n)` returning the 32-bit unsigned integer formed by reversing the bits of `n`.
concept: Peel off each bit from the low end of `n` and place it at the mirrored position from the high end of the result — always process a fixed 32 positions since leading zeros of `n` still matter in a fixed-width reversal.

title: Sum of Two Integers
prompt: Write `solve(a, b)` returning `a + b` without using the `+` or `-` operators.
concept: XOR gives the sum of each bit position without carrying, and AND-then-shift-left gives the carry to add in next; repeat until there's no carry left. Python's unbounded ints need masking to 32 bits so the loop actually terminates like it would in a fixed-width language.

title: Spiral Matrix
prompt: Write `solve(matrix)` returning all elements of `matrix` in clockwise spiral order.
concept: Shrink four boundaries (top/bottom/left/right) inward after tracing each side; the two guard checks before tracing the bottom row and left column stop a already-collapsed single row or column from being double-counted.

title: Rotate Image
prompt: Write `solve(matrix)` rotating the n x n `matrix` 90 degrees clockwise in place (no return value).
concept: Transpose the matrix (flip across the main diagonal) then reverse each row — that composition is exactly a clockwise rotation, and doing it in two simple in-place passes avoids needing a second buffer matrix.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
prompt: Write `solve(matrix)` that, if an element is 0, sets its entire row and column to 0, done in place (no return value).
concept: Zeroing cells as soon as a zero is found would cascade into zeroing more of the matrix than intended; first record which rows/columns contain a zero, then do a second pass to actually zero them out.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
prompt: Write `solve(s, k)` returning the length of the longest substring achievable by replacing at most `k` characters with any other character so it becomes all one character.
concept: Sliding window tracking the max single-character count seen inside it: the window is valid as long as (window size - max count) <= k, i.e. the non-majority characters all fit within the allowed replacements.

title: Minimum Window Substring
prompt: Write `solve(s, t)` returning the smallest substring of `s` that contains every character of `t` (with multiplicity); return `""` if none exists.
concept: Sliding window with a need-count map: expand right until every required character is covered, then greedily shrink left while it's still covered, recording the smallest valid window seen along the way.

title: Palindromic Substrings
prompt: Write `solve(s)` returning the total count of palindromic substrings of `s` (counting distinct positions, not distinct text).
concept: Expand around every possible center — n single-character centers and n-1 between-character centers — and count each successful expansion. This covers both odd- and even-length palindromes in O(n^2) without checking every substring from scratch.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
prompt: Write `solve(s)` returning the longest palindromic substring of `s`.
concept: Expand around every center (odd and even) and track the widest expansion seen; this is O(n^2) versus checking every substring's palindrome-ness independently which would be O(n^3).

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
prompt: Write `solve(list1, list2)` merging two sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list and returning its head.
concept: Use a dummy head node so the first real node doesn't need special-casing, then splice whichever list's current node is smaller onto the tail, advancing that list — a leftover tail from either list just gets attached whole at the end.

title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
prompt: Write `solve(head, n)` removing the nth node from the end of the linked list and returning the new head, in one pass.
concept: Two pointers spaced n apart: advance a lead pointer n steps first, then move both together until the lead hits the end — the trailing pointer now sits just before the node to remove. A dummy head avoids a special case when the head itself is removed.

title: Reverse Linked List
prompt: Write `solve(head)` reversing a singly linked list in place and returning the new head.
concept: Walk the list once, at each node flipping `next` to point at `prev` before advancing both — the classic three-pointer shuffle (prev, curr, next) that avoids losing the rest of the list when a link is rewritten.

title: Linked List Cycle
prompt: Write `solve(head)` returning whether the linked list has a cycle.
concept: Floyd's fast/slow pointers: advance one pointer by 1 and another by 2 each step; if there's a cycle they must eventually land on the same node, and if the fast pointer hits the end there's no cycle. No extra memory needed, unlike tracking visited nodes in a set.

title: Reorder List
prompt: Write `solve(head)` reordering the linked list in place from `L0->L1->...->Ln` to `L0->Ln->L1->Ln-1->...` (no return value).
concept: Three steps: find the middle with slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half, then merge the two halves by alternating nodes. Doing it in place without an array avoids O(n) extra space.

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
prompt: Write `solve(root)` returning the maximum depth (number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path) of a binary tree.
concept: A tree's depth is 1 plus the deeper of its two subtrees' depths, recursively — the classic bottom-up recursion where a `None` node contributes depth 0.

title: Same Tree
prompt: Write `solve(p, q)` returning whether two binary trees are structurally identical with the same node values.
concept: Recurse on both trees together: they match if both are `None`, or both exist with equal values and matching left/right subtrees. Any mismatch in shape or value short-circuits to False immediately.

title: Invert Binary Tree
prompt: Write `solve(root)` mirroring a binary tree (swap every node's left and right children) and returning the new root.
concept: Swap a node's children then recurse into both — order doesn't matter (swap-then-recurse or recurse-then-swap both work) as long as every node in the tree gets its children swapped exactly once.
