title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
prompt: Write `solve(root)` returning the node values level by level (top to bottom, left to right within a level) as a list of lists.
concept: BFS with a queue, processing one full level at a time by snapshotting the current queue length before pushing that level's children — mixing recursion (DFS) in without tracking depth would interleave levels incorrectly.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
prompt: Write `solve(root)` returning whether a binary tree satisfies the BST property (every node's value strictly between bounds set by its ancestors).
concept: Pass down a valid (low, high) range as you recurse, tightening it at each step — just checking a node against its immediate parent isn't enough, since a deep-right-then-left descendant must still respect an ancestor far above its parent.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
prompt: Write `solve(root, k)` returning the kth smallest value in a binary search tree (1-indexed).
concept: An inorder traversal of a BST visits values in ascending order, so the kth smallest is just the kth value emitted — no need to collect and sort every value first.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST
prompt: Write `solve(root, p, q)` returning the lowest common ancestor of nodes `p` and `q` in a binary search tree.
concept: Use the BST ordering instead of generic tree search: if both `p` and `q` are less than the current node, the LCA must be in the left subtree; if both greater, the right subtree; otherwise the current node is where their paths split, so it's the answer.

title: Subtree of Another Tree
prompt: Write `solve(root, subRoot)` returning whether `subRoot` appears anywhere in `root` as an exact subtree (same structure and values).
concept: Reuse a same-tree equality check at every node of `root`: `subRoot` is a subtree if it exactly matches the tree rooted at the current node, or is a subtree of either child — a small recursive helper composed with recursive descent.

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
prompt: Write `solve(preorder, inorder)` rebuilding and returning the root of the binary tree these two traversals came from.
concept: Preorder's first value is always the current subtree's root; find that value's position in inorder to know how many nodes fall in the left subtree, then split both lists at that point and recurse. A hashmap from value to inorder index turns each lookup into O(1) instead of a linear scan.

test_cases.expected_stdout: [3, [9, None, None], [20, [15, None, None], [7, None, None]]]

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
prompt: Write `solve(root)` returning the maximum sum along any path in the tree (a path may start and end at any node, doesn't have to pass through the root).
concept: Each node returns the best sum extending *downward* through just one child to its parent, but while recursing it also checks the best *through* itself using both children — those are two different quantities, and conflating them is the classic bug here. Negative subtree contributions get clamped to 0 (skip that branch) rather than dragging the sum down.

title: Merge k Sorted Lists
prompt: Write `solve(lists)` merging a list of k sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list and returning its head.
concept: A min-heap holding each list's current head lets you always pull the smallest value across all k lists in O(log k) instead of scanning all k heads every step. A tie-breaking counter in the heap entries avoids Python trying to compare ListNode objects directly when values tie.

title: Maximum Subarray
prompt: Write `solve(nums)` returning the largest sum of any contiguous subarray of `nums`.
concept: Kadane's algorithm: at each position decide whether extending the running subarray or starting fresh from here gives a bigger sum, tracking the best seen. O(n) versus checking every subarray's sum which is O(n^2).

title: Maximum Product Subarray
prompt: Write `solve(nums)` returning the largest product of any contiguous subarray of `nums`.
concept: Unlike sum, a negative number can flip a very negative running product into the new max, so track both a running max AND running min at each step (the min might become the max after multiplying by another negative).

title: Word Search
prompt: Write `solve(board, word)` returning whether `word` can be traced through adjacent (up/down/left/right) cells of `board` without reusing a cell.
concept: Backtrack from every starting cell, temporarily marking a visited cell (e.g. with a sentinel character) so it can't be reused deeper in the same path, then restoring it on the way back up so other starting points still see the original board.

title: Number of Islands
prompt: Write `solve(grid)` returning the count of islands (connected groups of '1's, connected up/down/left/right) in the 2D `grid` of '1'/'0' strings.
concept: Flood-fill (DFS or BFS) from every unvisited land cell, marking the whole connected island visited in one pass, then counting how many times a fresh flood-fill had to start — that count is the island count.

title: Course Schedule
prompt: Write `solve(numCourses, prerequisites)` returning whether all `numCourses` courses can be finished given `prerequisites` pairs `[course, prereq]`.
concept: This is cycle detection on a directed graph: DFS each course tracking three states (unvisited / currently-on-the-recursion-stack / fully-done) — revisiting a node that's still on the stack means a cycle, so the courses can't all be scheduled.

title: Clone Graph
prompt: Write `solve(node)` returning a deep copy of a connected undirected graph, given a reference to one of its nodes.
concept: DFS from the start node, keeping a hashmap from original node to its clone so each node is only cloned once — when a neighbor is revisited (which happens constantly in an undirected graph), reuse its clone from the map instead of recloning and looping forever.

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
prompt: Write `solve(heights)` returning every cell `[r, c]` from which water can flow to both the Pacific (top/left edges) and Atlantic (bottom/right edges) oceans, flowing only to equal-or-lower neighboring cells.
concept: Flow the search backwards from each ocean's border cells uphill (to equal-or-higher neighbors), marking two separate reachable sets — a cell that ends up in both sets can drain to both oceans. Searching forward from every interior cell would be far more expensive than starting from just the borders.

title: Word Search II
prompt: Write `solve(board, words)` returning all words from `words` that can be traced through adjacent (up/down/left/right) cells of `board` without reusing a cell.
concept: Build a trie of all target words first, then do one combined backtracking search over the board following trie edges — this shares work across words with common prefixes instead of re-running a separate word-search for each word.

title: Clickstream Event Pipeline
prompt: A mid-size e-commerce site wants to capture clickstream events (page views, add-to-cart, purchases) from its web and mobile apps. The data needs to power a near-real-time dashboard for the ops team and a daily batch pipeline for the analytics team. Design the system.
rubric: Asked about event volume/scale, what counts as "near-real-time" (seconds vs minutes), and existing infra before designing
Sources layer: instrumentation format and delivery guarantees (at-least-once vs exactly-once), ordering needs
Processing layer: justified batch vs stream choice (or a hybrid) rather than defaulting to one without reasoning
Storage layer: partitioning key choice for the event log and how it avoids hot-partition skew (e.g. a viral product spiking one partition)
Consumers layer: distinguished the dashboard's latency needs from the batch pipeline's, rather than treating them identically
Failure handling: what happens when a stream processor crashes mid-batch, and how events get replayed without duplicating results

title: Sharding a Multi-Tenant SaaS Database
prompt: A B2B SaaS product started on a single relational database. It now has thousands of tenants (customers) and the database is hitting scale limits. Design how to shard and/or replicate it.
rubric: Asked about tenant size distribution (a few huge tenants vs many small ones), read/write ratio, and consistency needs before designing
Partition key choice justified (tenant_id vs composite key) and addressed the hot-tenant skew problem (one giant customer overwhelming a shard)
Proposed a rebalancing strategy for when a shard outgrows its capacity or a new large tenant signs up
Replication topology choice (leader-follower vs leaderless) justified against the stated consistency needs
Addressed cross-shard queries or joins if the schema requires data from multiple tenants/shards
Failure handling: what happens when a shard's leader node goes down

title: Event Streaming Platform with Schema Evolution
prompt: Multiple teams at your company publish and consume events through a shared Kafka-like broker. Teams deploy independently and need to change event schemas over time without breaking each other. Design the system.
rubric: Asked how many producer/consumer teams, deployment cadence, and whether backward/forward compatibility is required, before designing
Chose and justified an encoding format (e.g. Avro/Protobuf vs plain JSON) with schema evolution in mind
Addressed how a schema registry (or equivalent) enforces compatibility at write time and/or read time
Distinguished backward-compatible changes (e.g. adding an optional field) from breaking changes and how each gets rolled out
Addressed what happens to events already on the log when the schema changes later
Failure handling: what happens when a consumer receives a message in a schema version it doesn't recognize

title: Analytical Store for a Growing OLTP Workload
prompt: Your product's OLTP Postgres database handles transactions fine, but analytical/reporting queries from the BI team are timing out and slowing down the transactional workload. Design a solution.
rubric: Asked about query patterns (ad hoc vs fixed dashboards), data freshness requirements, and data volume before designing
Proposed separating the analytical workload from OLTP (e.g. replicate/CDC into a warehouse or column store) rather than just tuning the OLTP database
Justified column-oriented storage for the analytical side and why it suits aggregate queries over wide tables
Addressed how data moves from OLTP into the analytical store (batch ETL vs CDC) and the freshness tradeoff of that choice
Addressed schema design for analytics (e.g. star schema/denormalization) versus the normalized OLTP schema
Failure handling: what happens if the ETL/CDC pipeline falls behind or breaks

title: Change Data Capture Pipeline for a Sharded OLTP Store
prompt: A payments company needs to replicate every row change from its sharded OLTP database into a downstream data warehouse in near-real-time, without ever double-counting a transaction even if the replication process crashes and restarts mid-stream. Design the CDC pipeline.
rubric: Asked about acceptable replication lag, transaction volume, and what double-counting would actually break (e.g. a ledger balance) before designing
CDC mechanism choice justified (log-based CDC off the DB's write-ahead log/binlog vs. trigger-based vs. polling) with its tradeoffs acknowledged
Idempotent write strategy at the destination (upsert by transaction id, not blind append) so a crash-and-restart can't double-apply a change
Addressed how the pipeline tracks progress per shard (offsets/checkpoints) so a restart resumes exactly where it left off, not from the beginning or an arbitrary point
Addressed schema drift: what happens when a shard's table schema changes mid-stream
Failure handling: what happens when one shard's CDC stream falls behind the others

title: Lakehouse Ingestion with Late-Arriving Mobile Events
prompt: A mobile app buffers analytics events locally and syncs them whenever the device regains connectivity — sometimes hours or days late. Design the ingestion and aggregation pipeline so that daily aggregate reports (e.g. daily active users, revenue) are still correct even when a meaningful fraction of events for 'yesterday' arrive after today's report has already run.
rubric: Asked how late is 'late' in practice (minutes vs days) and whether reports can be corrected retroactively before designing
Proposed an explicit watermark or allowed-lateness policy for closing an aggregation window, rather than assuming all of a day's events arrive by midnight
Addressed what happens to events that arrive after the watermark/lateness cutoff (dropped, added to a correction batch, or trigger a recompute)
Distinguished a fast best-effort report from a later corrected/final report if the design uses that pattern, and how consumers know which one they're looking at
Storage/format choice supports cheaply mutating historical partitions (e.g. a table format with upserts) rather than requiring a full rewrite for every late correction
Failure handling: what happens if a burst of very old events (e.g. a device offline for a month) arrives all at once

title: Backfilling a Multi-Stage Pipeline After a Bug Fix
prompt: A transformation step three stages into a five-stage daily pipeline (ingest → clean → enrich → aggregate → serve) had a bug for the last 30 days, corrupting output at every stage downstream of it. Design how the orchestration system detects this, backfills correctly, and reduces the chance the same class of bug propagates silently again.
rubric: Asked whether all 30 days need reprocessing or just some, and whether downstream consumers can tolerate serving stale/corrected data during the backfill, before designing
Proposed a DAG-aware backfill (re-running only the buggy stage and everything downstream of it, per affected day) rather than reprocessing the entire pipeline from scratch
Addressed how the backfill avoids racing with the pipeline's regular daily run for the same day/partition
Addressed idempotency: reprocessing day N's data overwrites/replaces bad output rather than appending duplicate rows
Proposed a concrete detection mechanism (data quality checks between stages) that would have caught this sooner than 30 days
Failure handling: what happens if the backfill itself fails partway through the 30-day range

title: Exactly-Once Billing: Lambda or Kappa?
prompt: A billing pipeline charges customers based on metered usage events. It needs to reprocess a full day of events if a pricing bug is found, without double-charging anyone. You must pick ONE architecture: a Lambda architecture (separate batch + speed layers, merged at query time) or a Kappa architecture (single streaming layer, replayed from a durable log for reprocessing). State your choice and defend it.
key_points: Picks Kappa for a single code path (no batch/speed-layer drift) fed by a durable, replayable log — or Lambda for a genuine reason (e.g. very different batch-vs-real-time correction logic), not by default
Explains reprocessing concretely: replaying the log from an offset, not just 'streaming handles it'
Names idempotent writes (upsert by event id, not append) as the mechanism that makes replay safe without double-charging
Acknowledges the real cost of the other option (Lambda's dual-codebase maintenance burden, or Kappa's requirement that the log retain enough history to replay from)

title: Hash Sharding vs. Range Sharding for a Multi-Tenant DB
prompt: You're sharding a multi-tenant database by tenant_id across 16 shards. Tenant sizes vary wildly — a handful of enterprise tenants are 100x the size of a typical tenant. Choose hash-based sharding (hash(tenant_id) % N) or range-based sharding (contiguous tenant_id ranges per shard), and defend it.
key_points: Picks hash sharding for even distribution across small/medium tenants and explicitly flags that a single giant tenant still creates a hot shard either way — the choice doesn't solve that on its own
Names a mitigation for the giant-tenant case specifically (e.g. splitting one tenant across sub-shards, or a dedicated shard for outliers) rather than ignoring the stated skew
If choosing range sharding, justifies it via a concrete need (range scans across tenants, easier rebalancing by moving contiguous ranges) rather than picking it by default
Mentions rebalancing cost: hash sharding requires consistent hashing or a lookup layer to add shards without reshuffling everything; range sharding can split a range without touching others

title: Avro vs. Parquet for a Schema-Evolving Event Log
prompt: You're choosing a serialization/storage format for an event stream that a schema registry enforces backward-compatible evolution on. Consumers read individual events in near-real-time AND analysts later run columnar aggregate queries over months of historical events. Pick Avro or Parquet as the primary format for the raw event log, and defend it.
key_points: Recognizes these solve different problems: Avro is row-oriented and schema-evolution-friendly for per-record streaming reads/writes, Parquet is column-oriented and built for scan-heavy analytical queries
Picks Avro for the raw/streaming log specifically because of per-event write pattern and tight schema-registry integration, not just 'it's the standard for Kafka'
Proposes converting to Parquet downstream (e.g. in a batch/Silver layer) for the analytical workload instead of forcing one format to serve both patterns
Notes the cost of the wrong choice: Parquet's column layout makes single-record streaming writes/reads inefficient; Avro's row layout makes scanning one column across millions of records wasteful

title: Synchronous Multi-Region Replication vs. Async
prompt: A transactional OLTP database needs a replica in a second region for disaster recovery. Choose synchronous replication (commit waits for the replica to ack) or asynchronous replication (commit returns immediately, replica catches up), and defend it.
key_points: Ties the choice to the actual requirement: synchronous only if zero data loss (RPO=0) is a hard requirement despite the latency cost of a cross-region round trip on every write
Picks async as the default for most cases and explicitly names the tradeoff being accepted: a window of potential data loss on failover, bounded by replication lag
Addresses failover behavior concretely: what happens to in-flight/unreplicated writes if the primary dies mid-lag
Mentions that synchronous cross-region replication measurably raises write latency for every transaction, not just during failover

title: Batch ETL vs. CDC for Keeping an Analytical Store Fresh
prompt: An OLTP Postgres database feeds a columnar analytical store. The analytics team wants dashboards that reflect OLTP changes within minutes, not the current nightly batch. Choose scheduled batch ETL (more frequent) or Change Data Capture (CDC) streaming the write-ahead log, and defend it.
key_points: Picks CDC for minute-level freshness and explains why shrinking a batch window (e.g. hourly) doesn't cleanly get there — batch still re-scans/re-diffs full tables or needs fragile incremental logic
Names a concrete CDC mechanism (reading the WAL/replication slot) rather than vaguely saying 'stream the changes'
Addresses what happens if the CDC pipeline falls behind or breaks: does it need a backfill/replay story from the WAL or a snapshot, and does downstream stay consistent while it catches up
Acknowledges CDC's added operational complexity (schema drift on the source table, replication slot management) as a real cost, not just an upgrade with no downside

title: At-Least-Once Delivery: Dedup at the Consumer or the Broker?
prompt: Your event broker guarantees at-least-once delivery, so consumers can receive the same message more than once (e.g. after a consumer crash and rebalance before committing an offset). You must pick ONE place to guarantee idempotent processing: dedup logic in each consumer (checking a processed-ids store before acting), or a broker/gateway layer that filters duplicates before consumers ever see them. State your choice and defend it.
key_points: Picks consumer-side idempotency (each consumer stores processed ids and does an idempotent upsert) as the robust default, since a broker-side dedup layer can itself fail or introduce its own duplicate window — or defends broker-side dedup for a specific reason (e.g. many downstream consumers that can't be trusted to implement dedup correctly)
Explains the mechanism concretely: a unique event id plus an upsert/conditional-write pattern, not just 'we'll dedupe it'

Names the tradeoff: consumer-side pushes the correctness burden onto every consumer team (repeated effort, risk one team gets it wrong) vs. broker-side adds a stateful bottleneck and its own duplication risk
Acknowledges the processed-ids store itself needs a retention/expiry policy or it grows unbounded

title: Schema Registry Enforcement: Reject at Write Time or Read Time?
prompt: Your team runs a schema registry for events published across dozens of independently-deployed services. You must pick ONE place to enforce schema compatibility: reject non-compatible schema changes at write time (a producer can't publish until the registry accepts the new schema), or allow any write and let consumers handle unexpected/incompatible messages at read time. State your choice and defend it.
key_points: Picks write-time enforcement as the default (catches a breaking change before it reaches any consumer, at the cost of blocking a producer's deploy) — or defends read-time tolerance for a specific reason (e.g. consumers already handle unknown fields for other reasons, or the registry can't be a blocking dependency)
Distinguishes backward-compatible changes (e.g. adding an optional field) that should be allowed by default from breaking changes (removing/renaming a required field) that should be rejected
Explains what happens to old messages already on the log when the schema changes — read-time tolerance is still needed for historical data even under write-time enforcement
Names the cost of the chosen approach: write-time enforcement makes the registry a hard dependency for every deploy; read-time tolerance means bugs surface at runtime instead of deploy time

title: Data Quality Checks: Block the Pipeline or Alert and Continue?
prompt: An upstream table starts feeding your pipeline null values in a column that's never had nulls before. You must pick ONE policy for what a data quality check does when it detects this kind of anomaly: hard-fail the pipeline run (block downstream from seeing the bad data) or let the run continue and just alert on-call. State your choice and defend it.
key_points: Picks a policy based on blast radius/reversibility (e.g. hard-fail for anything feeding a financial or exec-facing metric, alert-and-continue for lower-stakes internal tables) rather than one blanket rule for everything
Explains the cost of hard-failing: it can cascade (a downstream job that depends on this one also misses its SLA) and needs a clear unblock/override path, not just 'stop'
Explains the cost of alert-and-continue: bad data reaches consumers and may need a costly backfill/correction later once someone acts on the alert
Names a concrete detection mechanism (e.g. null-rate/volume/schema anomaly thresholds compared against a rolling baseline), not just 'we'll monitor it'

title: Kafka Partition Count for Peak Clickstream Ingest
prompt: Your clickstream pipeline ingests 50,000 events/sec at peak, each event ~1KB. Kafka brokers on this cluster comfortably sustain ~10MB/s of write throughput per partition. Estimate how many partitions you need on the raw events topic to handle peak load, with reasonable headroom for skew and growth.
explanation: Peak throughput ≈ 50,000 events/sec × 1KB ≈ 50MB/s. At ~10MB/s per partition that's 5 partitions as a bare minimum; interviewers want to see you add headroom for hot-key skew and future growth, landing around 8-12 partitions rather than the razor-thin minimum.

title: Daily Compressed Storage Footprint for Raw Event Landing
prompt: The same clickstream pipeline averages 10,000 events/sec over a full day (well below its 50,000/sec peak), each event ~1KB raw, and Parquet with compression runs roughly 4x smaller than the raw JSON. Estimate the compressed daily storage added to the S3/ADLS raw layer, in GB/day.
explanation: 10,000 events/sec × 86,400 sec/day ≈ 864M events/day × 1KB ≈ 864GB raw/day. Divide by ~4x Parquet compression ≈ ~200GB/day compressed. Getting the order of magnitude right (hundreds of GB/day, not TB or MB) is what matters here, not the exact figure.

title: Read QPS for the Ops Dashboard's Key-Value Store
prompt: The clickstream ops dashboard is viewed by ~200 concurrent analysts, each polling for updated aggregates every 5 seconds. Estimate the read QPS the dashboard's key-value store (e.g. DynamoDB/Redis) needs to sustain.
explanation: 200 concurrent viewers each polling every 5s ≈ 200 / 5 = 40 reads/sec baseline. The real point of this estimate is noticing it's trivially low next to the ~50,000 events/sec ingest side — the dashboard's KV store is never going to be your bottleneck, so don't over-engineer it.

title: Per-Tenant Write QPS for a Multi-Tenant SaaS Shard
prompt: Your multi-tenant SaaS has 5,000 tenants. The top 1% of tenants (heavy users) generate 40% of total write traffic, and total write traffic across all tenants averages 8,000 writes/sec. Estimate the average write QPS a single heavy tenant in that top 1% generates, assuming even distribution within that group.
explanation: Top 1% of 5,000 tenants = 50 tenants, generating 40% × 8,000 = 3,200 writes/sec combined → 3,200 / 50 ≈ 64 writes/sec per heavy tenant. That per-tenant number is what tells you whether plain hash-sharding is enough or whether hot tenants need dedicated shard isolation.

title: Realistic vs. Worst-Case Ingest QPS for a Streaming Platform
prompt: A streaming platform onboards 200 producer services, each publishing at most 500 events/sec at peak, though in practice only about 20% of services are near peak at any given moment. Estimate the platform's realistic peak aggregate ingest QPS (not the theoretical worst case where every producer peaks simultaneously).
explanation: Naive worst case = 200 × 500 = 100,000 events/sec, but that assumes every producer peaks at the exact same instant, which real traffic rarely does. Using the given 20% concurrent-peak assumption: 0.2 × 200 × 500 ≈ 20,000 events/sec is the more realistic capacity-planning number — distinguishing theoretical worst-case from realistic correlated load is exactly what this drill is testing.

title: Processed-Event ID Store Size for Exactly-Once Dedup
prompt: Your pipeline ingests 50,000 events/sec at peak and guarantees idempotent processing by checking each event's UUID (16 bytes) against a processed-ids store before acting, retaining ids for a 24-hour dedup window. Estimate the store's size in GB needed to hold one day's worth of ids.
explanation: Naive raw math: 50,000 events/sec × 86,400 sec/day ≈ 4.32 billion events/day × 16 bytes/UUID ≈ 69GB just for the raw ids — before any KV-store per-key overhead (hash index entries typically add several bytes to tens of bytes per key), which pushes a real deployment closer to 100-150GB for a single day's window. At this scale a raw id-per-key store often isn't the right primitive at all — recognizing that a Bloom filter or similar probabilistic structure trades a small false-positive rate for a huge space savings is exactly the realization this drill is testing for.

title: Raw Retention Storage for Kappa-Style Full Replayability
prompt: To support a Kappa-style architecture, you want to retain 90 days of history on a Kafka topic so any bug can be fixed by replaying from the start of the retention window. The topic peaks at 50,000 events/sec (each event ~1KB), but average sustained throughput is roughly 40% of peak. Estimate the raw storage in TB needed for 90 days of retention, ignoring replication factor.
explanation: Average throughput ≈ 0.4 × 50,000 events/sec × 1KB ≈ 20MB/s. Over 90 days: 20MB/s × 86,400 sec/day × 90 days ≈ 155TB raw. This is before Kafka's typical replication factor of 3, which would roughly triple the real cluster footprint — the point of the drill is recognizing that a 'just replay from the log' architecture has a real, ongoing storage cost that scales with retention window, not a one-time or free decision.

title: RAG Pipeline for Customer-Support Docs
prompt: A company wants to let customers ask natural-language questions against their internal support docs (product manuals, past tickets, FAQs) and get accurate, cited answers instead of browsing pages themselves. Design the retrieval-augmented generation system.
rubric: Asked about doc volume/update frequency, acceptable latency, and whether answers need citations before designing
Chunking strategy justified (size, overlap, structure-aware splitting) rather than an arbitrary fixed size
Embedding model and vector index choice justified, plus a plan for re-embedding when docs or the model change
Retrieval layer: how top-k / re-ranking is tuned, and what happens when nothing relevant is retrieved (say unsure vs guessing)
Grounding: answers are tied back to retrieved sources with citations, and hallucination risk is explicitly addressed
Freshness: how the index stays in sync as docs are added, edited, or deleted

title: Tool-Use Loop for a Coding Agent
prompt: A team wants an agent that can take a natural-language coding task, then autonomously read files, run tests, and edit code across multiple steps until the task is done. Design the agent's tool-use loop and surrounding infrastructure.
rubric: Asked about the tool surface (which tools: file read/write, shell, test runner), autonomy level, and failure tolerance before designing
Loop structure: how the agent decides to continue vs stop (task complete, budget exhausted, no progress detected)
Tool-call safety: validation/sandboxing of tool inputs before execution, especially for destructive tools
Guarded against infinite loops or repeated-failure retries (max iterations, progress checks, error-pattern detection)
Context management: how prior steps/tool outputs are summarized or trimmed so the context window doesn't overflow on long tasks
Failure handling: what happens when a tool call errors unexpectedly or returns something the agent doesn't understand

title: LLM Serving Layer with Model Fallback
prompt: A product depends on an LLM API for a user-facing feature. The team wants a serving layer that stays fast and available even when the primary model provider is slow, rate-limited, or down, without blowing the budget. Design it.
rubric: Asked about latency SLA, traffic volume/spikiness, and budget constraints before designing
Model tiering/fallback strategy justified (cheaper/faster model or cached response vs waiting on the primary)
Caching strategy for repeated or near-duplicate requests, and what's safe to cache vs not
Handles rate limits/timeouts from the provider gracefully (backoff, circuit breaker, queueing) rather than surfacing raw errors to users
Cost/latency tradeoff made explicit for each fallback tier, not just correctness
Failure handling: what the user sees when every tier fails

title: Eval Pipeline for Catching Prompt Regressions
prompt: A team ships frequent small changes to a production prompt (and occasionally swaps the underlying model). They keep shipping fixes for one complaint that silently break a different use case. Design a system to catch regressions before they reach production.
rubric: Asked what quality dimensions matter (accuracy, tone, refusal behavior, latency) and how failures are currently discovered before designing
Offline eval set: how it's built/maintained (golden examples, categories covered) and kept representative over time
Automated scoring approach justified (exact match vs LLM-as-judge vs human review) with its tradeoffs acknowledged
Versioning: prompts and eval results are tracked together so a regression can be bisected to a specific change
Production monitoring: some signal (user feedback, sampled review, drift metrics) catches regressions that offline evals miss
Rollout safety: how a prompt/model change ships (shadow testing, canary, gradual rollout) rather than all-at-once

title: Real-Time Fraud Detection Pipeline
prompt: A payment processor handling 5,000 credit-card transactions per second needs a fraud detection system that returns a risk score in under 100ms before each transaction is authorized. False positives block legitimate revenue; false negatives lose money. Design the pipeline.
rubric: Identified that sub-100ms latency is the non-negotiable constraint and designed every component around it rather than treating it as one requirement among equals
Ingestion layer: Kafka or Kinesis partitioned by a key that enables locality (e.g. merchant_id) without creating hot partitions
Feature computation: stateful processing (Flink or similar) for velocity counts, amount deviation, geo-velocity — kept in a low-latency store (Redis) rather than recomputed per request
Scoring layer: lightweight model serving (ONNX, TF Serving) called synchronously from the authorization path, not a separate async job
Feedback loop: labeled review outcomes flow back into daily batch retraining, with a tunable threshold per merchant to control false-positive rates
Failure mode: what happens when the feature store or model server is unavailable — fail-open (authorize anyway) vs fail-closed (decline) and the revenue implications of each

title: IoT Sensor Data Platform
prompt: A company has 1 million IoT devices (industrial sensors, fleet GPS trackers) each sending a reading every 5 seconds — temperature, vibration, location. They need per-device anomaly detection (alert when a reading deviates 3-sigma from the rolling hourly mean), a real-time dashboard, and historical storage for 30 days of raw data. Design the platform.
rubric: Asked about device protocol constraints (MQTT vs HTTP), payload size, and whether devices support backpressure or retry before designing
Ingestion: MQTT broker (EMQX, HiveMQ) as the device-facing endpoint bridged to Kafka, acknowledging that IoT devices use constrained protocols
Processing: stateful streaming (Flink/Spark) maintaining per-device rolling statistics (1M devices × ~1KB state = ~1GB, fits in RocksDB-backed state)
Alerting: anomaly detection triggers notifications without creating a notification-storm when 10K devices spike simultaneously — deduplication and rate-limiting strategy
Storage: time-series database (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB) for recent data partitioned by device_id + time, cold archive to Parquet on S3 for data older than 30 days
Failure mode: how the system handles a device that goes offline for 48 hours then reconnects and floods its backlog without starving other devices' processing

title: Server Log Aggregation at Scale
prompt: A SaaS company runs 10,000 servers each generating 50,000 log lines per second (500 bytes average). Engineers need to search error/warning logs from the last 7 days with sub-second latency, and occasionally forensically query debug logs from months ago. Design the log aggregation system.
rubric: Started with the scale calculation (500M lines/sec, 250GB/sec ingestion) and let the numbers drive architectural decisions rather than ignoring throughput
Ingestion: lightweight agents (Fluent Bit over Fluentd for memory footprint) shipping to a large Kafka cluster with partitioning by service name and NVMe storage
Hot/cold tier design: errors and warnings indexed in Elasticsearch or ClickHouse (7-day retention, sub-second search); debug logs sampled or written to Parquet on S3 with Athena for forensic queries
Explicitly addressed what gets dropped at peak — at 250GB/sec, indexing everything is cost-prohibitive, so sampling or tiered retention is mandatory and justified
Processing: a streaming job (Flink) that parses, enriches (hostname, region, deploy version), and routes logs by severity with different quality-of-service guarantees per path
Failure mode: what happens when the Elasticsearch cluster falls behind or a broker fails during a sustained ingestion peak — backpressure, shedding, and replay strategy

title: Food Delivery Order Processing State Machine
prompt: A food delivery platform processes orders through a complex state machine: order placed → restaurant accepts → preparing → driver assigned → picked up → delivered. Each state transition is an event, multiple microservices are involved, and orders can fail at any step (restaurant rejects, driver cancels, food goes cold). Design the event-driven order processing system.
rubric: Identified the core challenge as managing a distributed state machine with exactly-once guarantees across microservices rather than proposing a monolithic order table
Eventing layer: Kafka topics per state transition (OrderPlaced, OrderAccepted, DriverAssigned, etc.) with the Outbox Pattern to atomically commit DB writes and event publishes
State materialization: a streaming job (Flink) that reads the event log and materializes the current state of every active order into a fast serving store (Redis) for the customer tracking screen
Timeout handling: a scheduler or timer service publishes timeout events when a step doesn't complete within SLA (e.g. restaurant doesn't respond in 3 minutes → auto-cancel)
Failure mode: what happens if the driver app crashes mid-delivery — GPS heartbeat monitoring detects the gap and reassigns without duplicating the delivery
Exactly-once: acknowledged that true exactly-once across arbitrary services is impossible and proposed effectively-once through idempotent event handlers keyed on event ID

title: Feature Store for Batch Training and Real-Time Inference
prompt: An ML team needs a feature platform that serves both batch training (reading millions of historical feature vectors daily) and real-time inference (reading a single feature vector in under 10ms at p99). Features include streaming aggregations (logins in the last 24h) and batch computations (lifetime purchase total). Features must be consistent — a model trained on Tuesday must use the same feature values it would see at inference on Wednesday. Design the feature store.
rubric: Identified the dual-serving-path constraint (offline for training, online for inference) and designed two distinct stores rather than forcing one store to serve both
Offline store: partitioned by entity_id + event_timestamp in Delta Lake or similar, supporting point-in-time-correct joins to prevent training-serving skew
Online store: Redis or DynamoDB keyed by entity_id holding only the latest feature values, with TTL-based expiry and sub-5ms read latency
Feature pipeline: streaming features computed by Flink dual-writing to both stores; batch features computed by Spark and backfilled to both stores with versioning
Consistency guarantee: explicitly addressed point-in-time joins so training data exactly matches what inference would have seen — the core correctness property of a feature store
Failure mode: what happens when the online store is unavailable during inference — fallback to default values, stale cache, or fail-open, and how each affects model accuracy

title: Ride-Sharing Data Model for Analytics
prompt: A ride-sharing company wants to build an analytics data model to understand driver onboarding conversion (signup → document approval → activation → first trip) and trip performance (request → offer → accept → pickup → complete). Data analysts need to query driver funnel metrics and trip conversion rates. Design the dimensional model.
rubric: Enumerated core entities (Driver, Rider, Vehicle, Offer, Trip, Payment, Rating, Location) before designing any tables — scoped the model before diving into columns

SCD strategy justified: explained why each dimension uses Type 1, Type 2, or Type 3 based on query patterns (e.g. current status for driver onboarding is Type 1, historical address changes for regulatory reporting are Type 2)
Fact grain: stated the grain of each fact table explicitly (one row per trip request, one row per completed trip) and designed columns that respect that grain without fan-out

Driver onboarding funnel: modeled milestone timestamps (signup, docs_submitted, docs_approved, activated, first_trip) as columns in the driver dimension rather than a separate event table — justified by simple current-value query patterns
Trip conversion: demonstrated a SQL approach (LEFT JOIN offer→trip with CASE WHEN count logic) rather than hand-waving the metric definition
Missing dimension self-audit: identified geo/location as a needed dimension when prompted, and explained what queries it enables (trip density, high-profit regions)

title: Synchronous Dual-Write vs. Log-Based Materialization for a Feature Store
prompt: Your feature store needs to keep the online store (Redis, sub-5ms reads) and offline store (Delta Lake, historical queries) consistent. Option A: the streaming job dual-writes to both stores synchronously — the feature is only considered written after both succeed. Option B: the streaming job writes only to Kafka; a separate consumer materializes the online store, and a batch job materializes the offline store from the same log. Which do you choose and why?
key_points: Dual-write consistency: synchronous writes guarantee the online and offline stores are always consistent, but double the write latency and make the pipeline vulnerable to partial failures (one store down blocks the other)
Log-based materialization decouples the write paths — the online store can be updated in near-real-time while the offline store catches up on a batch schedule, and a Kafka outage doesn't block either
Read-your-write consistency is the real constraint: if a model trains at 2pm, does it need features from a 1:59pm event that's still propagating to the offline store?
Operational complexity: dual-write needs distributed transaction semantics or a saga; log-based needs idempotent consumers and handles replay naturally

title: Fail-Open vs. Fail-Closed for Real-Time Fraud Scoring
prompt: Your fraud detection model server times out or returns an error during a 100ms transaction authorization window. Option A: fail-open — authorize the transaction anyway and flag it for async review. Option B: fail-closed — decline the transaction and let the customer retry. Which do you choose and why?
key_points: Fail-open maximizes revenue and customer experience (legitimate transactions go through) but lets through every fraudulent transaction during the outage window
Fail-closed protects against fraud losses during the outage but blocks legitimate transactions, hurting merchant relationships and customer trust
The decision depends on fraud-to-false-positive cost ratio: for high-value finance (wire transfers) fail-closed is standard; for low-value e-commerce (coffee purchases) fail-open is common
A hybrid approach is tunable per merchant based on their historical fraud rate and transaction amount — high-risk merchants get fail-closed, low-risk get fail-open

title: Per-Device vs. Aggregated Timers for IoT Anomaly Detection
prompt: For 1 million IoT devices, you need to detect when a device's reading deviates from its own recent history. Option A: maintain per-device rolling statistics in Flink state (1M entries, ~1GB of state). Option B: bucket devices by type/location and detect anomalies at the bucket level using aggregate statistics. Which do you choose and why?
key_points: Per-device state is more accurate (catches individual device degradation) but costs ~1GB of Flink state plus checkpointing overhead at 1M keys
Bucket-level aggregation is cheaper in state and compute but misses individual device failures if only one device in a large bucket degrades
The right answer depends on what kind of failures matter: slow calibration drift (per-device needed) vs. plant-wide outages (bucket detects fine)
A tiered approach is often best: bucket-level for real-time alerting, per-device for offline investigation, with the Flink job doing bucketing and a separate batch job computing per-device stats

title: Airflow Executor: Celery vs. Kubernetes vs. Local
prompt: You need to pick an Airflow executor for a data platform running 500 DAGs with a mix of lightweight Python operators and heavy SparkSubmit operators. Option A: CeleryExecutor with a fixed pool of worker nodes. Option B: KubernetesExecutor with dynamic pod-per-task scaling. Option C: LocalExecutor on a single beefy instance. Which do you choose and why?
key_points: CeleryExecutor offers predictable capacity with a fixed worker pool but suffers from static over-provisioning (paying for idle workers) or under-provisioning (backlogs during peak), and needs separate infrastructure (Redis/RabbitMQ) to manage

KubernetesExecutor spins a pod per task — ideal for heterogeneous workloads where a lightweight Python operator needs 0.5GB and a Spark operator needs 8GB, but adds K8s networking overhead, slower pod startup, and requires K8s expertise to tune
LocalExecutor is simple and free but runs everything on one node — a single memory-hungry task OOMs the scheduler and takes down unrelated DAGs, unsuitable beyond ~50 DAGs or any Spark workload

The right choice depends on workload diversity and team skills: Celery is the safe default for uniform-medium workloads, K8sExecutor wins for heterogeneous workloads with existing K8s investment, LocalExecutor is a dev-only choice

title: COPY vs. MERGE for Incremental Warehouse Loads
prompt: Loading 10M new rows daily into a 500M-row fact table. Option A: COPY (append new data into a new partition, then swap). Option B: MERGE INTO (upsert new rows into the existing table in place). Which do you choose and why?
key_points: COPY + partition swap is idempotent, fast, and doesn't deadlock — you load into a staging table, validate, then swap the partition in a metadata-only operation. But it requires proper partitioning and means the table is briefly missing the newest partition during the swap
MERGE INTO is atomic and doesn't require partitioning but is slower (full table scan to find matches), risks deadlocks under concurrent loads, and is harder to roll back if the merge is wrong
COPY wins for large append-only fact tables with date-based partitioning (most common pattern), while MERGE is better for smaller dimension tables that need true upsert and can tolerate slower writes
Some warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery) have materialized-table-swap that combines both — always worth mentioning as a 3rd option

title: Identity Resolution Pipeline
prompt: Three legacy systems each identify customers differently: the e-commerce platform uses email, the support tool uses a session cookie, and the mobile app uses a device ID. The same person appears under different identifiers across systems. The marketing team needs a unified customer 360 for campaign attribution, and the data team needs to merge analytics without double-counting. Design the identity resolution pipeline.
rubric: Identified that identity resolution is a probabilistic/graph problem, not a simple JOIN — same person appearing as three different IDs requires pairwise matching with confidence scoring
Ingestion: collected all identifiers from every source into a single event stream keyed by whatever ID the source provides, preserving raw pairs for re-resolution

Resolution strategy: deterministic rules (matching email) for high-confidence links, probabilistic (name + address fuzzy match, device graph) for lower-confidence edges, with a manual review queue for borderline cases
Storage: an identity graph (Neo4j or a purpose-built ID service) mapping source IDs to canonical profiles, with versioning so historical queries can use the resolution that was live at the time

Reconciliation: a scheduled batch job that re-resolves the graph as new data arrives (an email added to a device-ID profile can merge two previously separate canonical profiles), with conflict-resolution rules for when profiles merge
Failure mode: what happens when two profiles auto-merge incorrectly — a rollback mechanism to split merged profiles without losing the event history that was attributed to the merged profile

title: GDPR-Compliant Data Deletion Pipeline
prompt: A data platform stores user activity across a data lake (Parquet on S3), a data warehouse (Snowflake), and a real-time serving layer (Redis). When a user exercises their right to be forgotten (GDPR Article 17), their personal data must be deleted from all storage tiers within 30 days. However, the business still needs aggregate analytics and must retain an audit trail proving deletion was performed. Design the deletion pipeline.
rubric: Distinguished between hard delete (PII fields scrubbed) and soft delete (canonical user record replaced with a tombstone, aggregates preserved) rather than treating all data as equivalently deletable

Identified the core tension: deletion destroys the ability to retroactively compute correct aggregates including that user — proposed either pre-deletion snapshotting or accepting permanent aggregate approximation

Implementation: a deletion request queue (Kafka topic keyed by user ID) consumed by per-layer deletion jobs — S3 uses rewrite-with-exclusion, Snowflake uses UPDATE/DELETE with masking, Redis uses DEL with TTL confirmation
Audit trail: a deletion-log table recording what was deleted, when, and by which request ID, retained separately from user data and not subject to deletion itself
Verification: a post-deletion scan that confirms no residual PII for the deleted user exists in any layer, with periodic re-scans for backup/archive copies that may have been missed
Failure mode: what happens when a deletion job partially fails (S3 succeeds, Snowflake fails) — a compensating transaction or a retry queue with exactly-once semantics per layer

title: Data Lake Access Control and Governance
prompt: A company consolidated all its data into a single S3 data lake with a Databricks/Trino query layer. A marketing analyst accidentally queried the HR salary table because nothing prevented them from seeing it. The security team now demands a least-privilege access model: every user should see only the datasets their role entitles them to, and all access must be auditable. However, the data lake is unstructured — thousands of tables, no consistent tagging. Design the access control system.
rubric: Identified that the hard problem is classification (knowing what data exists and what sensitivity level it has), not enforcement — without tagging, you can't write access rules
Classification strategy: automated (scan for PII patterns: email regex, salary column names, SSN patterns) plus a curator workflow for manual tagging, with a default-deny for unclassified data
Enforcement: three-layer — S3 bucket policies for coarse access, Unity Catalog / Lake Formation for table/column-level grants, and a query proxy that rewrites SELECT * to exclude masked columns
Audit: all queries logged with user identity, query text, rows returned, and timestamp, with an anomaly detector for access patterns outside normal baselines
Operations: self-serve access request workflow with automated approval for low-sensitivity data and manual approval for PII, all recorded in the audit log

Failure mode: what happens when a new table lands without a classification tag — deny-by-default prevents access, so a 'quarantine zone' with temporary 48-hour auto-access during classification processing
